title: Could a bigger tile fit if its side may be a fraction?
description: The plan of the twelve by sixteen room is tiled again, this time with sides that need not be whole numbers of feet. The tile counts along the two walls must be whole numbers in the ratio three to four, and the smallest such counts give the longest side. Keeko's doubt, a tile that fits one wall only, is tested on the plan.
teaching_notes: One idea: whole tile counts on the two walls keep the ratio of the walls, so the longest tile comes from the smallest counts. Watch for students who test one wall only and call a tile fitting.

source: What if the tile side could be a fractional number of feet?
video_script.why: The child has found the largest whole-number tile and now asks whether a fractional side could do better.
video_script.substitution: A tile of any side fits when whole tile counts fill each wall, and those two counts share the ratio of the two walls.
video_script.anchor: The room of the book, twelve feet by sixteen feet, and tiles whose side may be a fraction of a foot.
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko says a six feet tile fits the twelve feet wall exactly, twice, so it works. But along sixteen feet it fits twice and leaves four feet, so it does not fit the room.
video_script.payoff_line: No tile larger than four feet can fit.

final_answer.spoken: no, the largest tile is still four feet

names.Ziva: builds a new house and tiles the main room (12 ft by 16 ft)

maths_rules: A tile of side s fits exactly when 12 = m x s and 16 = n x s for whole numbers m and n.
So m : n = 12 : 16 = 3 : 4, and m = 3k, n = 4k for a whole number k.
The side is s = 12 / (3k) = 4 / k, which is largest when k = 1, so s = 4 ft with 3 and 4 tiles.
Slip: a 6 ft tile fits 12 ft twice, but 16 = 6 + 6 + 4 leaves 4 ft over; 6 does not divide 16.
video_script.design: One idea: the whole counts on the two walls keep the ratio three to four, so the longest tile has three and four tiles. Assumes ratios of two numbers. Wrong idea: checking one wall only. The plan stays all video.

<bookmark mark='room'/>The room is twelve feet by sixteen feet. This time the side of a tile may be a fraction of a foot.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>Could a square tile with a side longer than four feet still fit the room exactly?

narration: <bookmark mark='fit'/>A tile of any side fits a wall exactly when a whole number of tiles fills it.
<bookmark mark='more'/>The smaller the tile, the more tiles the wall needs. The longer the tile, the fewer tiles it needs.

beats.on_screen: To find: can a tile longer than 4 ft fit both walls exactly?

marks.find: The words To find are written under Given

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find whether a tile longer than four feet can fit both walls exactly.

narration: <bookmark mark='counts'/>Step one, let the short wall hold some whole number of tiles, and the long wall another. The same tile must fit both walls exactly.

beats.on_screen: Step 2: m to n = 12 to 16 = 3 to 4

marks.ratio: The counts are tied to the lengths
marks.reduce: The ratio twelve to sixteen is written and reduced to three to four

narration: <bookmark mark='ratio'/>Step two, the counts follow the lengths, because the tile is the same. <bookmark mark='reduce'/>The ratio of twelve to sixteen is three to four. The counts must be in that ratio.

beats.on_screen: Step 3: smallest whole counts 3 and 4; side = 12 / 3

marks.side: The side is written as twelve divided by three

narration: <bookmark mark='small'/>Step three, fewer tiles mean a longer side. The smallest whole counts in this ratio are three tiles and four tiles.
<bookmark mark='side'/>Divide the short wall of twelve feet by three tiles to get the side.

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>No tile larger than four feet can fit.
Smaller fractional tiles fit too, but they need more tiles.

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks a six feet tile fits, because it fills the short wall exactly, twice.
<bookmark mark='gap'/>Along the long wall, two such tiles cover only twelve feet. Four feet is left over.
<bookmark mark='fix'/>That gap is too small for another tile. A tile must fill both walls exactly.
